summary: Specifies an extension of OSPFv3 for mobile ad hoc networks, called OSPF-MDR. It adds a MANET interface type that relies on a connected dominating set of routers for flooding. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF-MDR adapts OSPFv3 for wireless networks where routers may move and may not all be within direct radio range. It selects some routers to relay updates and connect the others, reducing repeated messages and unnecessary router-to-router sessions.

questions: what is a manet designated router
what is a connected dominating set
subtitle: OSPFv3 selects a connected set of routers to reduce flooding and adjacency work on mobile wireless networks.

tldr.problem: Existing OSPF interface types have scaling and convergence problems in mobile ad hoc networks, where routers may not all hear one another directly.
tldr.mechanism: OSPF-MDR adds a MANET interface. Routers use neighbor information to select MANET Designated Routers and Backup MDRs, which limit flooding and the adjacencies that routers must form.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5614 is Experimental and has been updated by RFC 7038 and RFC 9454. Its design also allows a choice between smaller partial-topology advertisements and full topology information.

today: RFC 5614 is Experimental and has been updated by RFC 7038 and RFC 9454. Consult those documents for later changes to the OSPF-MDR specification.

sections.title: Why OSPF Needs a MANET Interface
sections.content:
RFC 5614 defines OSPF-MDR, an extension of OSPFv3 for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). A MANET is a broadcast-capable wireless network with multiple hops, where routers and hosts can move. The extension can also be used on non-mobile mesh networks that use layer-3 routing.

The RFC identifies three problems with existing OSPF interface types in MANETs: flooding does not scale well, Designated Router election may not converge in every situation, and point-to-multipoint interfaces can create many adjacencies. OSPF-MDR reduces the number of routers that flood new link-state advertisements and the number of router pairs that become adjacent.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF-MDR is for wireless networks where routers may move and may not all hear one another directly. It reduces how many routers repeat network updates and how many pairs must set up a close routing relationship.

sections.title: MDRs, Backup MDRs and Parents
sections.content:
Each MANET router uses neighbor information to decide whether it is an MDR, a Backup MDR (BMDR), or an MDR Other. MDRs form a connected dominating set (CDS): every router either belongs to this connected set or is one hop from it. If the network itself is biconnected, MDRs and BMDRs together form a biconnected CDS for added robustness.

A non-MDR selects a neighboring MDR as its Parent and becomes adjacent with it. With biconnected adjacency enabled, an MDR Other can also select a Backup Parent. MDRs and BMDRs form the backbone adjacencies; this avoids requiring every neighboring pair to exchange databases. A neighbor is routable only after the router has a route to it and the neighbor meets the required quality condition.
sections.plainLanguage: A connected set of selected routers keeps the network linked, and each other router attaches to a selected neighbor called its Parent. Backup MDRs add alternate relays when the network and settings support that extra connection.

sections.title: How Routers Select the MDR Set
sections.content:
The selection algorithm runs separately on every MANET interface. It compares each router with its bidirectional neighbors using Router Priority, current MDR Level, and Router ID, in that order. A larger tuple is preferred, which tends to keep existing MDRs in place and reduce new adjacency setup.

A router becomes an MDR when higher-priority neighbors do not already provide the required short paths through the local neighborhood. The MDRConstraint parameter sets the hop limit used by this decision. A router that is not selected as an MDR may become a BMDR unless the other routers provide the required two node-disjoint paths. The algorithm uses two-hop neighbor information carried in Hellos.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router compares its priority and role with nearby routers. It joins the MDR set when the higher-ranked routers nearby cannot already connect the neighborhood within the configured hop limit.

sections.title: Hellos, Adjacencies and LSA Flooding
sections.content:
OSPF-MDR adds link-local signaling data to OSPFv3 Hello packets. Full Hellos report neighbor information; differential Hellos report recent changes. These messages give routers the two-hop neighborhood information used by the selection algorithm. The extension also uses additional data in Database Description packets to identify MDR roles and parents.

Only selected router pairs form adjacencies when adjacency reduction is enabled. When an MDR receives a new link-state advertisement (LSA), it normally floods it on the MANET interface. A BMDR waits for the configured backup interval and floods only when it finds a neighbor not already covered by another router that forwarded or acknowledged the LSA. MDR Others do not flood an LSA back through the interface on which they received it. Retransmission to adjacent routers supports reliable flooding.
sections.plainLanguage: Hellos tell routers which neighbors are reachable and what changed. MDRs repeat new routing updates; Backup MDRs wait briefly and repeat an update only when nearby routers may have missed it.

sections.title: Topology Detail and Security Choices
sections.content:
Routers can advertise a partial or full view of MANET links in their router-LSAs. The minimal setting reduces flooding overhead but does not guarantee shortest paths. Other settings add links to support shortest paths or redundant routes; all routers must choose one of the specified shortest-path settings for shortest-path routing to be guaranteed. The default uses partial-topology LSAs that support shortest paths and reduced adjacencies.

The RFC describes using the IPv6 Authentication Header or Encapsulating Security Payload for authentication, integrity, or confidentiality. Wireless links can make interception, traffic analysis, interference, spoofing, falsification, and overload attacks easier. The described manual keying uses the same key on all routers in a MANET, so compromise of one router can expose the others to impersonation.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can send less topology detail to reduce overhead, but the smallest setting may produce routes that are not shortest. Security protection can help, though the shared manual key creates risk if one router is compromised.

viz.caption: THE THREE ROUTER ROLES ON A MANET INTERFACE

items.label: MDR
items.desc: Selected router that participates in the connected dominating set and normally floods new LSAs.

items.label: Backup MDR
items.desc: Backup flooding role when neighboring MDRs may not have reached every neighbor.

items.label: MDR Other
items.desc: Neither an MDR nor a Backup MDR; does not flood an LSA back on the receiving interface.
